candidateRows: Naturalists can construct a comparably explanatory worldview without adding God, regardless of the broad shape of causal reality.
This states the naturalist's governing comparative case: adding God does not improve explanation across alternative structures of causal reality.
Oppy replaces isolated premise-conclusion arguments with a developed naturalistic worldview intended to show that no explanatory topic requires adding God.
The problem of evil gives theism no local advantage if its alleged advantage merely presupposes that naturalism already failed to explain minds elsewhere.
The example supplies a rule against double-counting alleged explanatory failures and supports Oppy's whole-worldview method of comparison.
The claim that evil poses a greater explanatory problem for naturalists than for theists.
Oppy argues that explanatory topics must be assessed across the complete worldview, so a supposed theistic advantage concerning evil cannot simply import a dispute about minds.
Worldview comparison permits reasonable disagreement because explanatory coverage and theoretical simplicity require judgment rather than yielding a decisive algorithmic result.
This qualifies the intended force of Oppy's naturalist case and defines the comparative epistemic standard governing the debate.
The moderator's suggestion that naturalism simply dominates theism by matching its explanations with greater simplicity.
Oppy says observers may reasonably balance explanatory success and simplicity differently, especially when evaluating a worldview distant from their prior commitments.
Arguments remain useful for identifying considerations that favor theism or naturalism even though no agreed algorithm determines the uniquely correct balance of worldview virtues.
This establishes Pearce's method and explains how his subsequent arguments can provide comparative support without claiming mechanically decisive proof.
Oppy's position that reasonable evaluators may balance explanatory virtues differently without reaching a decisive resolution.
Pearce accepts that worldview virtues require complex balancing but maintains that arguments can reveal genuine comparative advantages and guide the development of each worldview.
The contingent total causal history requires an explanation that is both non-causal and non-necessitating, which naturalism lacks but divine free grounding can provide.
This is Pearce's principal comparative argument that classical theism possesses an explanatory resource unavailable within science-oriented naturalism.
Oppy's assertion that naturalism can duplicate any explanatory structure proposed by theism.
Pearce shifts from explaining contingent objects to explaining the totality of causal occurrences, arguing that no member of that totality can causally explain the whole.
Creation should be understood as grounding, in which God's creative activity is the more fundamental reality that unifies and explains the created world.
The grounding account supplies the specific non-causal explanatory relation required by Pearce's argument concerning the total causal history.
Pearce characterizes grounding as more fundamental reality giving rise to less fundamental reality, illustrates it, and then applies that structure to divine creation.
A necessary initial state plus necessary but indeterministic evolution can naturally explain a contingent history without any additional non-natural ground.
This directly contests the claimed explanatory asymmetry by constructing a naturalistic account that yields contingent history from necessary conditions.
Pearce's claim that naturalism has no explanation of history that is both non-necessitating and explanatorily complete.
Oppy grants that naturalism offers no transcendent ground but argues that indeterministic evolution from a necessary initial state explains why some contingent history occurs.
Necessary initial conditions and laws still call for deeper explanation, and unexplained brute necessities can be explanatorily worse than brute contingencies.
This denies that labeling the naturalist's foundations necessary completes the explanation and identifies their bruteness as a comparative theoretical cost.
Oppy's proposal that necessary initial reality and necessary indeterministic evolution adequately explain contingent history.
Pearce raises possible incompleteness or circularity and argues by analogy that unexplained necessity does not remove explanatory deficiency merely by making a fact unavoidable.
Postulating a necessary God does not eliminate explanatory bruteness unless the theist can explain divine necessity using resources unavailable to the naturalist.
The challenge turns Pearce's demand for deeper explanation back on theism and questions whether the proposed divine ground improves the explanatory stopping point.
Pearce's contention that the naturalist's necessary starting point remains an unexplained and eliminable theoretical cost.
Oppy asks what could explain God's necessity if the naturalist account is rejected for failing to explain its own necessary starting point.
Explanatory inquiry may legitimately terminate in autonomous facts, with real and nominal definitions providing plausible cases that do not stand in need of explanation.
This supplies Pearce's account of legitimate explanatory termination and begins explaining how theism might avoid an arbitrary brute stopping point.
Oppy's challenge to explain the necessity of God rather than leaving divine necessity as another unexplained starting point.
Pearce distinguishes brute facts from autonomous facts and argues that definitions of words and things are candidates for truths to which requests for further explanation do not apply.
A maximally satisfying explanation requires an ultimate entity whose real definition or essence entails its actual existence, and God is a promising candidate.
This supplies Pearce's proposed route from the demand for an ultimate explanation to a necessarily existent, non-naturalistic reality.
Pearce distinguishes his proposal from an ontological argument and presents essence-entailing-existence as the structure needed to avoid unexplained bruteness.
A naturalist can nominate the universe's initial state as the entity whose essence includes existence, so the proposed explanatory structure does not favor theism.
The objection contests the claimed comparative advantage by arguing that naturalism can occupy the same essence-based explanatory role.
Pearce's claim that an essence entailing existence favors a God-like ultimate reality.
Oppy accepts the real-definition framework for argument's sake but argues that the initial condition of the universe is also eligible for the required role.
Theism has simple, unified candidate definitions from which existence follows non-ad-hocly, while no comparably clear naturalistic candidate or definition is available.
This develops the comparative case that theistic ultimate realities possess better-defined candidates for necessary existence than naturalistic origins do.
Oppy's proposal that the universe's initial state could have an essence that includes existence.
Pearce appeals to multiple non-naturalistic real definitions and questions both the entity status of an initial singularity and the availability of a naturalistic definition.
Ignorance about reality beyond cosmic expansion leaves open that the unknown natural origin has existence in its essence, making exclusion of that possibility unwarranted.
The move attacks Pearce's asymmetry by arguing that present ignorance prevents ruling out a natural entity with the required necessary essence.
Pearce's contention that naturalism lacks an entity and real definition capable of grounding necessary existence.
Oppy emphasizes that neither side knows the pre-expansion reality and argues that this uncertainty preserves the naturalist's proposed explanatory possibility.
Although science could in principle disclose many kinds of ultimate reality, current scientific guidance offers no developed naturalistic analogue to theistic real-definition proposals.
The argument reframes the issue from bare possibility to the present comparative availability of rigorous candidates, yielding a claimed evidential advantage for theism.
Oppy's claim that an unknown natural origin may turn out to possess existence as part of its essence.
Pearce stresses responsible deference to science while arguing that speculative origin physics has not supplied a candidate matching several developed theistic definitions.
Theistic definitions must be examined for success rather than credited for development alone, since even perfect-being accounts may not entail necessary existence.
This directly undermines the asserted theistic advantage by separating the existence of a long-developed proposal from its adequacy as an explanation.
Pearce's claim that theistic traditions possess developed real definitions absent from naturalism.
Oppy uses disputes over perfection and necessity to argue that theistic candidates require substantive validation and cannot prevail merely through historical elaboration.
Default trust in human cognitive faculties and other people extends to the widespread practice of interpreting experiences as encounters with God or supernatural reality.
This introduces a distinct positive argument for theism based on epistemic consistency, testimony, and the presumptive reliability of religious experience.
Pearce adopts a broadly Reidian starting point of trust and argues that naturalism incurs special exceptions by classifying religious experiences as illusory or hallucinatory.
A broad category of religious experience is easily explained naturalistically, while a narrow evidentially stronger category raises doubts about how frequently such experiences occur.
The challenge targets both the classification and evidential force of the experiences on which Pearce's religious-experience argument depends.
Pearce's claim that widespread apparent experiences of God merit default epistemic trust.
Oppy contrasts ordinary church experiences with rarer extraordinary reports and asks which category supplies evidence that is both resistant to naturalism and sufficiently common.
Religious experience should be understood broadly but weighted by quality, with first-person experience providing non-neutral justification even amid disagreement.
The response preserves the breadth of the experiential evidence while explaining variable evidential weight and the special justification available to experiencers.
Oppy's dilemma between common but naturally explicable experiences and rare stronger religious experiences.
Pearce rejects a sharp boundary between mundane and extraordinary cases, distinguishes their evidential value, and argues that perceptual disagreement need not require neutrality.
Religious and atheistic experiences should receive context-sensitive testimonial weight, while naturalistic debunking accounts risk selectively distrusting religious faculties.
This answers the self-trust objection, concedes genuine experiential evidence against God, and restates the comparative consistency argument against naturalistic debunking.
Oppy's claim that Reidian trust does not justify preferring a religious interpretation over his own nonreligious response.
Pearce distinguishes interpersonal from self-trust, recognizes experiences of divine absence as counterevidence, and argues that debunking stories may presuppose religious unreliability.
Human faculties are not generally trusted without qualification; experience teaches us the circumstances in which each faculty is unreliable.
This challenges the epistemic framework supporting Pearce's treatment of religious experience by replacing presumptive general trust with learned, faculty-specific calibration.
Pearce's claim that naturalism treats religious experience as a special exception to general trust in human faculties.
Pearce had argued that naturalistic debunking displays unusually strong distrust toward religious experience compared with the broader attitude taken toward human faculties.
Theism can incorporate agency-detection mechanisms as faculties given by God to enable direct contact with God.
The proposal blocks an inference from a cognitive mechanism for agency detection to naturalism by showing that the same mechanism is compatible with a theistic causal story.
The naturalistic use of hyperactive agency detection as an explanation of religious experience and belief.
The exchange concerned whether cognitive-science accounts of religious belief support naturalism or instead presuppose that religious experiences are inaccurate.
Religious experience is commonly cultivated through learned practices analogous to perceptual and scientific investigation, so its nonspontaneity and disagreement do not undermine it categorically.
This supplies Pearce's principal response to irregular and conflicting religious experiences by defending their epistemic legitimacy through analogies with trained perception and scientific inquiry.
The objection that random, conflicting, culturally interpreted religious experiences look more like a natural faculty misfiring than divine communication.
Oppy had highlighted the irregular distribution, harmful outcomes, lack of novel information, and incompatible interpretations of religious experiences as evidence favoring naturalism.
The continual appearance of unsuccessful visionaries resembling successful religious founders weakens appeals to founders' transformative experiences.
The argument broadens the comparison class beyond successful traditions, challenging selection based on religious success and pressing a naturalistic explanation of visionary founders.
Pearce's use of figures such as Paul and Muhammad to compare revelatory founders with investigators who encounter something unexpected.
Pearce had argued that founders may undergo unsolicited experiences which initiate sustained communal practices resembling broader methods of investigating unfamiliar phenomena.
Sociological influences and disagreement make religion less reliable in degree than science, but do not establish a fundamental epistemic difference in kind.
This calibrated concession preserves the epistemic viability of religious inquiry while explaining why detailed theology deserves substantially less confidence than strong scientific theories.
Oppy's appeal to numerous similar visionaries whose movements fail despite circumstances resembling those of successful religious founders.
Oppy had stressed that new visionary movements arise frequently and that most founders resembling Joseph Smith do not succeed in launching enduring religions.
The disorder and ambiguity of religious experience fit nonintentional causes better than communication from an agent who intends relationship with human beings.
The argument turns experiential randomness into evidence bearing directly on theism: communicative confusion is less expected if a divine agent intentionally produces experiences to relate to people.
Pearce's analogy between religious traditions and scientific or perceptual practices for investigating difficult aspects of reality.
Pearce had maintained that religious and scientific inquiry differ mainly in degree, while conceding lower confidence in detailed theological conclusions.
Religious experience need not aim chiefly at uniform true theology and should be assessed through whole traditions, lived effects, testimony, and long-term communal functioning.
This revises the expected purpose of divine communication and offers a holistic epistemology intended to explain why diverse experiences may still have religious value under theism.
Oppy's contention that ambiguous and inconsistent experiences are unexpected if an intentional divine agent is trying to relate to humans.
Oppy contrasted confusing religious experience with ordinary interpersonal communication and argued that its pattern resembles nonintentional natural causation more closely.
The enduring diversity of radically different religious traditions resists a plausible single-religion account and is easier for naturalism to explain.
This directly compares the explanatory performance of naturalism and religious worldviews over the global diversity and durability of religious experience, matching the debate's central motion.
Pearce's proposal to evaluate well-developed religious traditions holistically by their experiences, practices, effects, and historical functioning.
Pearce had proposed examining entire mature traditions rather than expecting religious experiences primarily to generate shared, specific, true theological beliefs.
A long-isolated religious tradition might represent genuine experiences of God interpreted through its own framework rather than faculties wholly disconnected from reality.
The response identifies a theistic route for accommodating religious diversity without declaring entire traditions irrational or wholly non-truth-tracking, though it remains deliberately tentative.
Oppy's Rainbow Serpent example and claim that radically diverse enduring traditions are more easily explained by naturalism.
Oppy argued that the ancient Rainbow Serpent traditions differ sharply from Christianity, Hinduism, and Buddhism and frustrate any plausible unified religious explanation.
Widespread disagreement requires respect for others' rationality while still making greater general trust in one's own faculties unavoidable.
The conclusion states the governing epistemic principle used to reconcile persistent religious disagreement with continued commitment to one's own considered worldview.
The suggestion that pervasive disagreement among philosophers and religious traditions undermines confidence that any side is tracking reality.
The speakers had distinguished subjective rationality from truth-tracking and compared religious diversity with the similarly broad range of philosophical opinions.
